What is a law of composition on a set S?
column2:
A map S × S → S.
The image of (x, y) is written xy and called their product.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 3

column1: Give Lang's definition of a monoid.
column2:
A set with a law of composition that is associative and has a unit element.
It is never empty, since it contains e.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 3

column1: Prove in one line that a unit element is unique.
column2:
If e and e′ are both units, then e = ee′ = e′.
The first equality uses e′ as a unit, the second uses e.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 3

column1: Give Lang's definition of a submonoid.
column2:
A subset that contains e and is closed under the law of composition.
It is then a monoid under the induced law.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 6

column1: In Lang, almost all means what exactly?
column2:
All but a finite number.
He fixes the phrase here and relies on it for the rest of the book.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 5

column1: How does Lang define the product x1 ··· xn?
column2:
By induction, attaching each new factor on the right:
∏ν=1n xν = (x1 ··· xn−1)xn

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 4

column1: The n-fold product is defined by one bracketing. Which statement lets you bracket any way you like?
column2:
∏μ=1m xμ · ∏ν=1n xm+ν = ∏ν=1m+n xν
Lang leaves the proof as an exercise.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 4

column1: What is the empty product in a monoid, and what does that convention buy?
column2:
e.
It makes x0 = e fall out of the definition of powers, with no separate rule and no special case in xn+m = xnxm.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, pp. 4, 6

column1: Define ∏<sub>i∈I</sub> f(i) for an arbitrary index set I.
column2:
Let I₀ = {i : f(i) ≠ e}, and require f(i) = e for almost all i, so I₀ is finite.
Then ∏i∈I f(i) = ∏i∈I₀ f(i).

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 5

column1: ∏<sub>i∈I</sub> f(i) rests on two hypotheses. Name both, and say what each one buys.
column2:
f(i) = e for almost all i, which makes the product finite.
G commutative, which makes the value independent of the order.
Drop either and the symbol stops meaning anything.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 5

column1: State Lang's reordering theorem for products.
column2:
If G is commutative and ψ permutes (1, …, n), then
∏ν=1n xψ(ν) = ∏ν=1n xν.
This is the one result in §1 that Lang proves in full.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 5

column1: Outline Lang's proof of the reordering theorem in four moves.
column2:
1. Check n = 1, then assume the case n−1.
2. Pick k with ψ(k) = n.
3. Commute that factor to the far right end.
4. Reindex the rest by φ, which skips k, and apply the induction hypothesis.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 5

column1: How does Lang define x<sup>n</sup>, and what does it give at n = 0?
column2:
xn = ∏1n x, for every integer n ≥ 0.
At n = 0 the empty product gives x0 = e.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 6

column1: Which power law needs an extra hypothesis, and what is it?
column2:
(xy)n = xnyn needs xy = yx.
xn+m = xnxm and (xn)m = xnm hold in any monoid.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 6

column1: For subsets S, S′ of a monoid G, what is SS′, and what is GG?
column2:
SS′ is the set of all products xy with x ∈ S and y ∈ S′.
GG = G, because G has a unit element.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 6

column1: In Lang I §1, which results are proved and which are left as exercises?
column2:
Proved: reordering for commutative monoids (p. 5).
Exercises: general associativity (p. 4), the double-product rule over I and J (p. 6), and the formal power laws (p. 6).

Lang, Algebra, I §1

column1: Lang gives a monoid from topology in §1. What is it, and what is its unit element?
column2:
Homeomorphism classes of compact connected surfaces, added by connected sum.
The unit is the class of the ordinary 2-sphere.
Every class is uniquely nτ + mπ with n ≥ 0 and m = 0, 1, or 2.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, pp. 6–7

column1: Which monoid from §1 does Lang need later, and for what?
column2:
Multiplicative subsets of a commutative ring, meaning subsets that contain the unit element and are closed under multiplication.
Localization uses them in Chapter II, §4.

Lang, Algebra, I §1, p. 6
